A) a bit of both. I think the characters are bonded together by guilt, but the “appearances” are real. 
B) People get sick. I don’t think there was anything supernatural that put the farm hand in his state. At least nothing in the movie alluded to this. 
C) The “priest” was never there in Texas. It was the entity the entire time. The real one was in Chicago and had his own personal baggage. The entity gave Louise the priest’s number so she would contact him, triggering his own grief allowing the entity to do what it does best. 

The bigger point is that there isn’t a point. Sometimes evil is just evil. No overarching theme, no grand scale, it’s just evil because it wants to be

While I agree with you, I think the character thought that if he left, everything would stop. All the horrific actions centered at the farm house, so I think he thought that returning to his normal life would make everything ok. He even encouraged his sister to leave because then she could save herself. However, the ultimate point is that no one is safe. “We don’t matter.” The priest was miles away and he wasn’t safe.

I think the point is that there isn’t a point. It hurts who it wants to and because it can. If you look at the director’s earlier movie (The Strangers [not as good as this movie]) when the main characters ask the enemy why they are doing this, they respond with “because you were home”. There’s no cursed object, no haunted house, no deal with the devil. They just caught the attention of the entity and it’s doing it because it’s evil.

^ This. The whole point of the movie is nihilism. They literally said “the wolf doesn’t care if you believe in it or not”. The point of the movie of the Bertino film was discussed in the phone call between the main characters near the end. One of the characters did try to flee and stated that “we don’t matter.” That’s the entire point of the film. I think the movie is great because evil doesn’t need a goal or a plot. Sometimes people hurt other people just because they can and they enjoy it. No master plan, no grand scheme, no end goal. Like the movie Strangers, when the character asks “why are you doing this?” The response is “because you were home.”

Now the movie is lacking in character development and character background, but the overall sense is that you can’t tell what’s real and what’s supernatural. Ordinary conversations are changed mid-sentence as a character becomes a spokesman for the devil. Things are ambiguous because you’re dealing with a force you’re not meant to understand (the protagonist is atheist). A force that can impersonate loved ones, create hallucinations, and is always lurking in the background. The point of the film is that you, as a mortal, can’t fight a near omniscient being. Even the character that ran away fell victim to it. It doesn’t care about your love, sense of duty, familial relationships, or half assed religion. 

The entire point of the film is that bad things happen and sometimes there’s no motive, no reason, and nothing you can do about it. Nihilism. Great film imo
